newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND, EU REACH UNDERSTANDINGS ON TRADE DISPUTES.
newsitem.headline: POLAND, EU REACH UNDERSTANDINGS ON TRADE DISPUTES.

text.p: Poland and the EU have made progress towards resolving several trade disputes troubling the country's ties with the Western bloc it hopes to join soon, European Commissioner Hans van den Broek said on Friday.

He said that after two days of talks in Warsaw, the two had signed letters of understanding concerning Poland's protection of its oil and steel sectors, imports of car parts for assembly and on its recognition of EU certificates.
"I think we have made considerable progress with letters signed today in the oil, car and steel sectors and the important question of certification," he told a news conference.

But the commissioner, responsible for ties with eastern Europe, made clear Poland could not expect to delay vital economic and administrative changes, just because its EU entry was politically desireable, and urged it to speed preparations.
Van den Broek did not give details of the understandings, saying they had to be consulted with EU members, but added: "We are in agreement that unilateral measures should be avoided."
Polish Foreign Miniser Dariusz Rosati told the news conference the talks were marked by understanding and a desire to compromise.

The EU, especially during blunt Brussels talks with Rosati in July, accused associated state Poland of unjustifiably extending tariff protection of its fuels sector until the year 2000, while preparing for foreign competition, without even consulting the union.

It criticised a Polish deal with Daewoo allowing the South Korean firm to import into Poland 110,000 disassembled cars duty-free for two years and Poland's unwillingness to keep to a calendar for lifting duties on EU steel on January 1, 1997.
Long delays in Poland's procedures for accepting EU safety certificates for imported goods were also questioned.

Van den Broek, who during the visit said he expected Poland to join in 2002 at the earliest, added the EU saw Poland as a front-runner for membership and wanted it to be ready in time when talks began, probably at the end of 1997 or early 1998.
The commissioner said he appreciated the difficulty of restructuring Poland's steel industry, but said this was a process EU members had gone through and they could help.
Apart from know-how, the EU would consider assistance for steel, possibly involving the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the European Investment Bank.
"This could prevent maybe further protective measures unilaterally by the Polish government," he said.
He said Poland had agreed to speed up alignment with the EU of policies over certification.

Rosati, who says the EU has also been partly to blame for the disputes, said the Poles had raised issues including EU barriers to Polish farm exports and transport questions and the EU had promised to try to eliminate these problems.
